How this book matches your exam. This book follows the 0470 syllabus for 2027–2028. (Cambridge says there are "no significant changes" in the 2029–2030 version.) It covers Core Content Option B, Key Question 1: Was the Treaty of Versailles fair? It deals with the aims of the Big Three, why the victors did not get everything they wanted, the impact of the treaty on Germany up to the end of 1923, and whether the treaty could be justified at the time.

How you are examined

  • Paper 1 (2 hours, 60 marks, 40%): you answer two Core questions and one Depth question. Each question has three parts:
  • (a) 4 marks: describe;
  • (b) 6 marks: explain;
  • (c) 10 marks: "How far…?" or "How important…?", marked in levels.
  • Paper 2 (1 hour 45 minutes, 40 marks, 30%): a source-based paper on one prescribed core topic.

Unit 10 practises the Paper 2 source skills. The marking guides are our own.

Levels for 10-mark (c) questions (our guide, based on the Cambridge pattern):

  • Level 1 (1–2): general answer.
  • Level 2 (2–4): identifies or describes.
  • Level 3 (4–6): explains one side.
  • Level 4 (7–9): explains both sides.
  • Level 5 (10): explains both sides and reaches a supported judgement.

Unit 1 of 10: The Situation at the End of the War, 1918–19

Key ideas

  • The armistice was signed on 11 November 1918. Germany had not been invaded, so many Germans did not believe they had really been defeated.
  • The human cost of the war: about 9–10 million soldiers died.
  • France lost about 1.4 million men.
  • Large areas of north-east France and Belgium were devastated.
  • The Paris Peace Conference opened in January 1919.
  • The decisions were dominated by the "Big Three": Woodrow Wilson (USA), Georges Clemenceau (France) and David Lloyd George (Britain).
  • Italy (Orlando) took part at first.
  • Germany was not invited to the negotiations.
  • Public opinion in Britain and France demanded revenge and compensation.
  • The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.

Worked examples

(a)-style question, 4 marks: "Describe the situation in Europe at the end of the First World War."

Model points:

  • millions dead;
  • France devastated;
  • the Kaiser abdicated and Germany became a republic;
  • revolution in Russia;
  • fear that communism would spread;
  • public anger towards Germany.

Example 2: Germany was excluded from the talks. This later fed the claim that the treaty was a Diktat (a dictated peace).

Example 3: the Hall of Mirrors was where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871. Signing there was symbolic revenge for France.

10-mark exam-style question

"Public opinion was the most important influence on the peacemakers in 1919." How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [10]

Answer guidance:

  • Agree: Lloyd George won the December 1918 election on promises to "make Germany pay". Clemenceau faced French voters demanding security and revenge.
  • Disagree: the leaders' own aims mattered too: Wilson's idealism, France's security fears and Britain's trade interests. So did the fear of communism spreading, and the need to compromise with each other.
  • Level 5: reaches a supported judgement. For example: "Public opinion shaped Lloyd George's and Clemenceau's demands, but compromise and national interests decided the final terms."

Common mistakes

  1. Saying Germany helped negotiate the treaty.
  2. Getting the dates wrong. The armistice was in 1918; the treaty was signed in 1919.
  3. Treating the Big Three as if they all agreed.
  4. Writing narrative with no judgement.
  5. Leaving out the fear of communism.

Quick recall

  1. When was the armistice signed?
  2. Who were the Big Three?
  3. When was the treaty signed?
  4. Was Germany invited to the talks?
  5. About how many French soldiers died?

Answers: 1) 11 November 1918. 2) Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George. 3) 28 June 1919. 4) No. 5) About 1.4 million.
